(CNN) -- Sen. Hillary Clinton will stop telling an emotional story about a uninsured pregnant woman who died after being denied medical care, Clinton's campaign said. Sen. Hillary Clinton was repeating a story she heard from someone on the campaign trail. A hospital has raised questions over the accuracy of the story, and Clinton's campaign has said although they had no reason to doubt the story, they were unable to confirm the details. In the story, Clinton describes a woman from rural Ohio who was making minimum wage at a local pizza shop. The woman, who was uninsured, became pregnant. Clinton said the woman ran into trouble and went to a hospital in a nearby county but was denied treatment because she couldn't afford a $100 payment. In her speeches, Clinton said the woman later was taken to the hospital by ambulance and lost the baby. The young woman was then taken by helicopter to a Columbus hospital where she died of complications.  Watch why the story is raising questions » . The New York senator heard the story during a campaign visit to a family's living room in Pomeroy, Ohio, in late February. Bryan Holman was hosting the candidate and told Clinton the story. She has repeated it frequently since then. As recently as Friday night in Grand Forks, North Dakota, Clinton said she was "just aching inside" as she was listening to the story. "It is so wrong, in this good, great and rich country, that a young woman and her baby would die because she didn't have health insurance or a hundred dollars to get examined," she said. While Clinton never named the hospital in her speech, the woman she was referring to was treated at O'Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio. The hospital said the woman did indeed have insurance, and, at least at their hospital, she was never turned away. Hospital Chief Executive Officer Rick Castrop in a statement said, "we reviewed the medical and patient accounts of the patient" after she was named in a newspaper story about Clinton's stump speech. "There is no indication that she was ever denied medical care at any time, for any reason. We clearly reject any perception that we ever denied any care to this woman." A hospital spokesperson confirmed to CNN the woman had insurance. She said the hospital decided to come forward after people in the community began to question if they had denied her care. Clinton's speech accurately reflects what she was told that day, but the campaign admits they were not able to confirm the account. Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said, "She had no reason to doubt his word." "Candidates are told stories by people all the time, and it's common for candidates to retell those stories. It's not always possible to fully vet them, but we try. For example, medical records are confidential. In this case, we tried but weren't able to fully vet the story," he said. Elleithee added, "If the hospital claims it didn't happen that way, we certainly respect that, and she won't repeat the story." "She never mentions the hospital by name and isn't trying to cast blame. She tells this story because it illustrates the point that we have a very serious health care problem in America. That's a point very few people will dispute." E-mail to a friend .

Clinton had been repeating a story she heard from someone on the campaign trail. A hospital has since raised questions about the accuracy of the account, and Clinton’s campaign said that although it had no reason to doubt the story, it was unable to confirm the details.

In the story, Clinton describes a woman from rural Ohio who was earning minimum wage at a local pizza shop. The woman, who was uninsured, became pregnant. Clinton said the woman experienced complications and went to a hospital in a nearby county, but was denied treatment because she could not afford a $100 payment.

In her speeches, Clinton said the woman was later taken to the hospital by ambulance and lost the baby. The young woman was then flown by helicopter to a Columbus hospital, where she died of complications. Watch why the story is raising questions »

The New York senator heard the story in late February during a campaign visit in the living room of a family in Pomeroy, Ohio. Bryan Holman, who was hosting the candidate, told Clinton the story. She has repeated it frequently since then.

As recently as Friday night in Grand Forks, North Dakota, Clinton said she was “just aching inside” as she listened to the story.

“It is so wrong, in this good, great and rich country, that a young woman and her baby would die because she didn’t have health insurance or a hundred dollars to get examined,” she said.

Although Clinton never named the hospital in her speech, the woman she was referring to was treated at O’Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio. The hospital said the woman did, in fact, have insurance and that, at least at its facility, she was never turned away.

Hospital Chief Executive Officer Rick Castrop said in a statement that “we reviewed the medical and patient accounts of the patient” after she was named in a newspaper story about Clinton’s stump speech.

“There is no indication that she was ever denied medical care at any time, for any reason. We clearly reject any perception that we ever denied any care to this woman.”

A hospital spokesperson confirmed to CNN that the woman had insurance. She said the hospital decided to come forward after people in the community began questioning whether it had denied her care.

Clinton’s speech accurately reflected what she was told that day, but the campaign acknowledged that it was not able to confirm the account.

“She had no reason to doubt his word,” Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said.

“Candidates are told stories by people all the time, and it’s common for candidates to retell those stories. It’s not always possible to fully vet them, but we try. For example, medical records are confidential. In this case, we tried but weren’t able to fully vet the story,” he said.

Elleithee added, “If the hospital claims it didn’t happen that way, we certainly respect that, and she won’t repeat the story.”

“She never mentions the hospital by name and isn’t trying to cast blame. She tells this story because it illustrates the point that we have a very serious health care problem in America. That’s a point very few people will dispute.”

(CNN) — Hillary Clinton’s campaign said the senator will no longer use a moving account about an uninsured pregnant woman who allegedly died after being refused medical treatment.

Clinton had been recounting a story she was told while campaigning. However, a hospital has challenged parts of the account, and her campaign said that while it had no reason to question the person who shared it, it could not verify the details.

In Clinton’s version, the woman lived in rural Ohio and earned minimum wage at a local pizza restaurant. She became pregnant but had no health insurance. Clinton said the woman experienced medical problems and went to a hospital in a neighboring county, where she was supposedly turned away because she could not pay $100 for care.

Clinton said in speeches that the woman was later brought to the hospital by ambulance and lost the baby. The woman was then flown by helicopter to a hospital in Columbus, where she died from complications.

The New York senator first heard the account in late February during a campaign stop at a family’s home in Pomeroy, Ohio. Bryan Holman, who was hosting Clinton, told her the story, and she repeated it often afterward.

On Friday night in Grand Forks, North Dakota, Clinton said listening to the story had left her “just aching inside.” She added, “It is so wrong, in this good, great and rich country, that a young woman and her baby would die because she didn’t have health insurance or a hundred dollars to get examined.”

Although Clinton did not identify the hospital in her remarks, the woman in question had been treated at O’Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio. The hospital said the woman actually did have insurance and, at least at that facility, was never refused care.

Rick Castrop, the hospital’s chief executive officer, said in a statement that the hospital reviewed the woman’s medical and billing records after she was identified in a newspaper article about Clinton’s campaign speech. “There is no indication that she was ever denied medical care at any time, for any reason,” Castrop said. “We clearly reject any perception that we ever denied any care to this woman.”

A hospital spokeswoman also told CNN that the woman was insured. She said the hospital chose to speak publicly after local residents began asking whether it had denied the woman treatment.

Clinton’s campaign said her speeches accurately represented what she had been told, but acknowledged that the story had not been fully confirmed.

“She had no reason to doubt his word,” Clinton spokesman Mo Elleithee said.

“Candidates are told stories by people all the time, and it’s common for candidates to retell those stories,” he said. “It’s not always possible to fully vet them, but we try. For example, medical records are confidential. In this case, we tried but weren’t able to fully vet the story.”

Elleithee said that if the hospital says events did not happen as described, the campaign accepts that and Clinton will stop telling the story.

He added that Clinton never named the hospital and was not trying to assign blame. Instead, he said, she used the account to underscore what she sees as a major health care crisis in the United States — a point he said few people would challenge.

counterfactuals.output:
**Clinton drops campaign story about Ohio woman after hospital disputes account**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Sen. Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign said she will stop using a campaign-trail story about an uninsured pregnant Ohio woman who allegedly died after being denied hospital care, after the hospital involved challenged key parts of the account.

Clinton had told the story in recent appearances as an example of what she described as the human cost of the nation’s health care crisis. According to Clinton’s version, a pregnant woman in Ohio had been turned away from a hospital because she lacked insurance and could not pay, and both the woman and her baby later died.

But the hospital named in connection with the case said the account was not accurate.

In a statement, O’Bleness Memorial Hospital in Athens, Ohio, said it was legally and ethically obligated to treat emergency patients regardless of their ability to pay. The hospital said it had reviewed the case and found no evidence that the woman had been denied care because she was uninsured or unable to pay.

“We implore the Clinton campaign to immediately desist from repeating this story,” the hospital said, adding that the claim was “not based in fact.”

The woman, identified in local reports as Trina Bachtel, died last year after complications related to pregnancy. Her baby also died. Clinton said she had heard the story from a local official while campaigning in Ohio and used it to argue for expanding health insurance coverage.

After the hospital’s denial, Clinton campaign aides said the senator would no longer repeat the story unless and until the details could be confirmed.

“The story was told to Senator Clinton by a credible source, and she believed it to be true,” a campaign spokesman said. “Given questions that have been raised, she will not be using the story going forward.”

The campaign also said the broader point Clinton was making remains valid: that millions of Americans lack health insurance and often delay or forgo care because of cost.

Clinton has made health care a central issue in her bid for the Democratic presidential nomination, frequently contrasting her universal coverage proposal with the plan offered by Sen. Barack Obama. The disputed Ohio story had become one of her most emotional examples on the trail, drawing strong reactions from audiences before the hospital publicly objected.
